Key Takeaways

  • AO6 is worth 16 marks — 40% of the writing section. Technical accuracy is not optional; it is the difference between grades.
  • Go beyond full stops and commas. Use semicolons, colons, and dashes deliberately to show the examiner you control your punctuation rather than just using it.
  • Upgrade your vocabulary from basic (“good,” “bad”) to precise (“commendable,” “detrimental”) — but only use words you are confident about.

Key Takeaways

  • Engage at least three senses in your writing — most students default to sight only. Sound and smell are especially powerful for atmosphere.
  • “Show don’t tell”: convey emotion through action and detail, not direct statements. This is what the mark scheme calls “crafted” writing.
  • Avoid clichés. One original comparison (“the silence had weight”) is worth more than five stock phrases (“quiet as a mouse”).

Key Takeaways

  • Subject terminology means specialist language terms (simile, metaphor, semantic field, etc.) used to describe how writers craft their work. AO2 requires it to be “relevant” and “accurate.”
  • The four-part formula — Name the technique, Quote the evidence, Explore the connotation, Link to the wider effect — ensures you never stop at feature-spotting.
  • If you forget a term, describe the effect instead. Never let a missing term stop you from making a strong analytical point. The examiner rewards insight, not vocabulary alone.

Key Takeaways

  • Every article needs a headline, a hooking opening, well-structured body paragraphs, and a memorable ending — not an essay-style introduction and conclusion.
  • Use a variety of rhetorical devices across your paragraphs: rhetorical questions, statistics, anecdotes, direct address, and tricolons.
  • Show the examiner you know the form — a standfirst, byline, and topic sentences are the conventions that separate articles from essays.

Key Takeaways

  • A strong ending elevates your entire piece — plan it before you start writing, not as an afterthought.
  • The four main ending types are circular, twist, reflective, and ambiguous — each works best with certain kinds of stories.
  • Avoid clichéd endings like “it was all a dream” — examiners see these constantly and they suggest a lack of planning.

Key Takeaways

  • Every Paper 2 writing task specifies an audience, purpose, and form — identify all three before you start planning.
  • Your audience determines your register and content; your purpose determines your techniques; your form determines your conventions.
  • The AO5 mark scheme rewards writing that is “convincingly matched” to APF — this is not optional, it is the foundation of a top-level response.
